content: Prosopis cineraria is a small to medium-sized tree predominantly found in the Thar Desert of Rajasthan, India. It is also known by various names such as Ghaf in the United Arab Emirates, Khejri, Jand, Sangri in Rajasthan, Jand in Punjabi, Kandi in Sind, Sami, and Sumri in Gujarat. Its trade name is Kandi. Natural Habitat The tree thrives in dry and arid regions of Arabia and India, including Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab, Gujarat, Western Uttar Pradesh, and the drier parts of the Deccan Plateau, extending as far south as Tuticorin. It is typically found in areas with annual rainfall below 500 mm. The climate in its natural distribution areas is characterized by extremes of temperature, with very hot summers and severe winters, including frost during December and January. Maximum shade temperatures range from 40°C to 46°C, while minimum temperatures range from 9°C to 16°C. The tree is adapted to plains or gently undulating terrain and rarely extends into hilly regions. It has developed significant drought resistance and grows on a variety of soils, performing best on alluvial soils with mixtures of sand and clay. It is also found on moderately saline soils but struggles in highly saline conditions. Rural communities encourage its growth in agricultural fields, pastures, and community lands, as it does not negatively impact crop yields and instead improves grain yield and biomass production. Distribution Prosopis cineraria is a key indigenous tree species in the plains of Punjab, Western Rajasthan, and Gujarat. It is also common in Bundelkhand and the areas around Delhi and Agra. The tree is found in the dry parts of Central and Southern India, including Maharashtra (near Nasik), Andhra Pradesh, and Karnataka south of the Godavari River. Its range extends to West Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Iran. In the Indian Thar Desert, it represents the climatic climax vegetation along with Salvadora oleoides. It is often associated with species like Tecomella undulata, Capparis decidua, Maytenus emarginata, Zizyphus spp., and Salvadora spp. The density of Khejri increases from the western to the eastern parts of Western Rajasthan. It grows well in older and younger alluvial plains and sandy undulating plains. Its ability to access perched water and absorb moisture from rains through its foliage allows it to survive in extremely arid regions with as little as 100 mm of rainfall. Tree Characteristics Prosopis cineraria is a small to moderately sized evergreen thorny tree with slender branches armed with conical thorns and light bluish-green foliage. Its dark green leaflets provide a thin, light shade. The tree coppices profusely and is evergreen or nearly so, producing new leaves before summer. Its small yellow or creamy white flowers appear from March to May, followed by rapidly growing pods that reach full size in about two months. Historically, this tree has played a vital role in the rural economy of the arid northwest Indian subcontinent. As a legume, it enhances soil fertility and is a crucial component of the vegetation system. It is well-adapted to arid conditions, tolerating extreme climate variations and browsing by animals like camels and goats. In areas with goat browsing, young plants develop a bushy, cauliflower-like appearance. The tree is a strong light demander, and dense shade can kill its seedlings. It is drought-resistant and thrives in dry and arid conditions, earning the description of an aridity-loving tree. It is one of the few indigenous tree species that withstands the harsh conditions of the Rajasthan desert. Its root system is extensive and well-developed, with taproots reported to penetrate up to 35 meters deep, allowing it to secure moisture from deep soil layers. The tree is frost-resistant and can survive the hottest winds and driest seasons when other plants fail. Farmers value it for its economic benefits and regulate its population through agroforestry management. Utilization of the Species Prosopis cineraria provides high-quality construction wood used for house-building, including rafters, posts, scantlings, doors, windows, well construction, water pipes, and agricultural implements. It is also used for small turning work and tool handles. The tree is a significant source of fodder, especially during winter when other green fodder is unavailable in dry regions. Its leaves are highly nutritious and profitable for feeding livestock during the winter months. The pods, known locally as Sangar or Sangri, are sweet and used as fodder for livestock. Dried pods, called Kho-Kha, are consumed by humans during famines and are also a rich animal feed. The tree is a top feed species, providing nutritious and palatable green and dry fodder for camels, cattle, sheep, and goats, which are essential for desert livestock. Its wood has a high calorific value, making it an excellent fuel source. Lopped branches are used as fencing material. Use in Environmental Conservation The tree's deep taproot system minimizes competition with associated crops. Improved soil conditions and higher nutrient availability under its canopy enhance the growth of associated crops. Rural communities encourage its growth in agricultural fields, pastures, and community lands. Its extensive root system stabilizes shifting sand dunes and serves as a windbreak and shelterbelt in afforestation projects for dry areas. It fixes atmospheric nitrogen through microbial activity and adds organic matter to the soil through leaf litter decomposition, rejuvenating poor soils. In arid regions, it provides much-needed shade and shelter for farmers, cattle, and wildlife during the summer months. Its pods are consumed by various livestock and wildlife, including blackbuck and chinkara in Western Rajasthan. Medicinal Uses The flowers of Prosopis cineraria are pounded, mixed with sugar, and used during pregnancy to prevent miscarriage. The water-soluble extract of the stem bark exhibits anti-inflammatory properties. The tree produces gum during May and June. Its bark is dry, acrid, and bitter with a sharp taste, possessing cooling, anthelmintic, and tonic properties. It is used to treat leprosy, dysentery, bronchitis, asthma, leucoderma, piles, and muscle tremors. The smoke from its leaves is beneficial for eye troubles. The fruit is dry and hot, with a flavor that can cause biliousness and damage nails and hair. The pods are considered astringent in Punjab. The bark is used as a remedy for rheumatism, coughs, colds, and asthma and is recommended for treating snakebites and scorpion stings.
